front: Why is current, not voltage alone, the cause of electrical injury?
back: Current flowing through the body causes the harm, and the amount depends on voltage divided by body resistance (I = V / R). Voltage only matters because it pushes the current.

front: What is the perception threshold of current through the body?
back: About 1 mA, the level at which most people notice a faint tingle.

front: What is the let-go threshold and about what current is it?
back: The current above which a person cannot release a conductor because the hand muscles clamp. It is roughly 10 to 20 mA.

front: What current range can cause ventricular fibrillation?
back: Roughly 50 to 100 mA through the chest, and sometimes less for a long exposure. The heart quivers and stops pumping blood.

front: Calculate the body current for 120 V across 1,500 ohms.
back: I = V / R = 120 / 1,500 = 0.08 A, or 80 mA, which is in the fibrillation range.

front: Calculate the body current for 120 V across a dry 100,000 ohm path.
back: I = 120 / 100,000 = 0.0012 A, or 1.2 mA, a faint tingle.

front: Which part of the body holds most of its electrical resistance?
back: The outer layer of dry skin. Wet, sweaty, or cut skin can drop the path to 1,000 ohms or less.

front: Why is a hand-to-hand or hand-to-foot path especially dangerous?
back: The current crosses the chest near the heart, which raises the chance of fibrillation.

front: What is an arc flash?
back: A release of heat, light, and pressure when current jumps through air between conductors or to ground, forming a very hot plasma.

front: What is an arc blast?
back: The pressure wave and flying molten metal produced when copper vaporizes and the air heats suddenly during an arc fault.

front: What does an arc flash label usually show?
back: The voltage, arc flash boundary, incident energy at a working distance, and the PPE level or arc rating required.

front: In what unit is incident energy measured?
back: Calories per square centimeter (cal/cm2). The label gives the minimum arc rating of clothing to wear.

front: What does NFPA 70E cover?
back: Electrical safety in the workplace, including boundaries, arc flash, PPE, and work procedures. NFPA 70 is the NEC, which covers installations.

front: What does lockout/tagout do?
back: It keeps energy sources off during work: a lock holds the disconnect open and a tag names who applied it and why.

front: List the main steps of lockout/tagout in order.
back: Prepare, notify, shut down, isolate, apply lock and tag, release stored energy, then verify the circuit is dead.

front: Who may remove a personal lock?
back: Only the worker who placed it. A formal procedure exists for the rare case when the owner cannot be found.

front: What is a hasp used for?
back: A hinged device that lets several workers place their own locks on one disconnect.

front: What is the live-dead-live test?
back: Prove the meter on a known live source, test the circuit you will work on, then prove the meter again on the known source.

front: Which conductor pairs must you test on a three-phase panel?
back: Each phase to every other phase, each phase to neutral, and each phase to ground.

front: What do meter category ratings CAT III and CAT IV mean?
back: They name the part of the system where the meter is safe. CAT III suits panels and feeders, and CAT IV suits the service entrance.

front: Why is a non-contact voltage pen not enough to prove a circuit dead?
back: It can miss voltage through shielded cable or with a weak battery. Use it only as a screening check beside a rated meter.

front: What is the purpose of leather protector gloves over rubber gloves?
back: They shield the rubber from cuts, punctures, and abrasion that would create a path for current.

front: Why is polyester clothing a hazard near arc flash?
back: Synthetic fabric can melt into the skin and worsen burns. Wear arc-rated clothing instead.

front: What is the minimum clear working space depth in front of a 120/240 V panel under NEC 110.26?
back: 3 feet (36 inches), with a width of 30 inches or the equipment width if greater, and headroom of at least 6.5 feet.

front: What type of ladder is preferred for electrical work, and why?
back: Fiberglass, because wood absorbs moisture and aluminum conducts.

front: What should you do first when a coworker is stuck to an energized conductor?
back: Cut power at the nearest safe disconnect if you can do it safely, then call emergency services. Do not touch the person.

front: What do you do if the victim has no pulse after the power is off?
back: Start CPR and send for an automated external defibrillator (AED), since fibrillation is the usual cause of death in shock.

front: What kind of extinguisher is used on an electrical fire?
back: One rated for electrical fires, such as carbon dioxide or dry chemical. Never use water or foam on live equipment. De-energize first if safe.

front: Why must rings and watches be removed near energized parts?
back: Metal jewelry can bridge terminals or bus bars and cause deep burns or an arc.

front: A person stands in a wet basement. Why is the shock risk higher?
back: Wet skin and a damp floor lower the body path resistance, so the same voltage drives much more current.

front: Why should a stored charge be released during lockout?
back: Capacitors, springs, and raised loads can hold energy after power is off, so discharge, block, or ground them as the procedure requires.

front: What is matter?
back: Anything that has mass and takes up space.

front: What is an element?
back: A pure substance that cannot be broken into simpler substances by ordinary chemical means, such as copper or oxygen.

front: What is an atom?
back: The smallest piece of an element that keeps the identity of that element.

front: Name the three main particles of an atom and their charges.
back: Proton (positive), neutron (no charge), and electron (negative).

front: What decides which element an atom is?
back: The number of protons in its nucleus, called the atomic number.

front: What is the atomic number of copper?
back: 29. A neutral copper atom therefore has 29 protons and 29 electrons.

front: What is a valence electron?
back: An electron in the outermost shell of an atom. It is the loosely held one involved in conduction and bonding.

front: How many valence electrons do copper, aluminum, and silicon have?
back: Copper has 1, aluminum has 3, and silicon has 4.

front: What is an ion?
back: An atom that has lost or gained electrons and so carries a net charge. Losing electrons makes it positive, gaining makes it negative.

front: What are free electrons?
back: Valence electrons that break loose from atoms in a metal and drift through the structure, forming the cloud that carries current.

front: What is a conductor?
back: A material with many free electrons that lets current flow easily, such as copper, silver, gold, or aluminum.

front: What is an insulator?
back: A material that holds its electrons tightly and has almost no free electrons, such as rubber, glass, or porcelain.

front: What is a semiconductor?
back: A material such as silicon with 4 valence electrons that conducts poorly when pure but can be doped to control conduction.

front: Rank silver, copper, gold, and aluminum by conductivity.
back: Silver is best, then copper, then gold, then aluminum.

front: Why is copper used for building wire instead of silver?
back: Copper conducts almost as well as silver at a far lower cost and also resists corrosion and bends easily.

front: What is insulation breakdown?
back: A strong enough voltage forces current through an insulating material. Moisture, dirt, and age lower the breakdown voltage.

front: What is the rule for attraction and repulsion of charges?
back: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.

front: If a rubber rod gains electrons from wool, what are the charges?
back: The rod becomes negative and the wool becomes positive. Charge is moved, not created.

front: What is conservation of charge?
back: Charge is never created or destroyed, only moved. The total charge of an isolated system stays the same.

front: What is static electricity?
back: Electric charge that sits on an object and does not flow, such as the charge built up by walking on a carpet.

front: Why can static electricity be a hazard?
back: A spark can ignite flammable vapors or dust and can damage sensitive electronics without being felt.

front: What is the unit of electric charge and its symbol?
back: The coulomb, symbol C. The formula symbol for charge is Q.

front: How many electrons make one coulomb?
back: About 6.24 x 10^18 electrons.

front: What is the charge of one electron in coulombs?
back: About 1.6 x 10^-19 coulomb.

front: What happens to the force between two charges if the distance doubles?
back: It drops to one quarter, because force varies with the inverse square of distance (Coulomb's law).

front: State the formula for current in terms of charge and time.
back: I = Q / t, so Q = I x t. One ampere is one coulomb per second.

front: How much charge moves when 4 A flows for 30 s?
back: Q = I x t = 4 x 30 = 120 coulombs.

front: How many electrons are in 120 coulombs?
back: 120 x 6.24 x 10^18 is about 7.49 x 10^20 electrons.

front: How much charge passes when 20 A flows for 5 minutes?
back: Convert 5 minutes to 300 s. Q = 20 x 300 = 6,000 coulombs.

front: What is the difference between electron flow and conventional current?
back: Electron flow goes from negative to positive, the true direction of electrons. Conventional current is drawn from positive to negative and is used in most schematics.

front: Name the six common sources of voltage.
back: Friction, chemical action, magnetism, light, heat, and pressure. Chemical action and magnetism supply nearly all practical power.

front: What is voltage and what unit measures it?
back: The electrical push, or potential difference between two points, measured in volts (V).

front: Why does a bird on a single high-voltage wire stay safe?
back: Both feet are at the same voltage, so there is no potential difference across the bird and no current passes through it.

front: What is current and what is its unit?
back: The flow of charge past a point, measured in amperes (A). One ampere is one coulomb per second.

front: How is an ammeter connected to measure current?
back: In series with the circuit, so the current passes through it. A clamp-on meter avoids breaking the circuit.

front: What is resistance and what unit measures it?
back: The opposition to current flow, measured in ohms, symbol the Greek capital omega.

front: Why must power be off before measuring resistance?
back: The ohmmeter supplies its own small voltage, and a live circuit can damage the meter or give a false reading.

front: Write the formula for the resistance of a wire.
back: R = rho x L / A, where rho is the resistivity of the material, L the length, and A the cross-sectional area.

front: What are the resistivity values of copper and aluminum in ohm-circular mils per foot?
back: About 10.37 for copper and 17 for aluminum, at 20 degrees Celsius.

front: What is a circular mil?
back: The area of a circle one mil (0.001 inch) in diameter. Wire area in circular mils equals the diameter in mils squared.

front: What is the area in circular mils of a 0.1 inch round wire?
back: Diameter is 100 mils, so area = 100 x 100 = 10,000 circular mils.

front: Find the resistance of 100 ft of 12 AWG copper (6,530 cmil).
Find the resistance of 200 ft of 8 AWG aluminum (16,510 cmil).
What happens to wire resistance if the length doubles?
back: It doubles, since resistance is directly proportional to length.

front: What happens to wire resistance if the area doubles?
back: It is cut in half, since resistance is inversely proportional to area.

front: Does a higher AWG number mean a thicker or thinner wire?
back: Thinner. 14 AWG is thinner than 12 AWG, which is thinner than 10 AWG.

front: How does temperature affect the resistance of copper?
back: Resistance rises as temperature rises, because atoms vibrate more and scatter the drifting electrons.

front: What is a positive temperature coefficient?
back: The resistance of a material increases as it warms, as in metals. Carbon and some semiconductors have a negative coefficient.

front: Give the formula for resistance at a new temperature.
back: R2 = R1 x [1 + alpha x (T2 - T1)]. For copper alpha is about 0.00393 per degree Celsius.

front: A copper winding is 4.00 ohms at 20 C. What is it at 75 C?
What is conductance and its unit?
back: G = 1 / R, the ease of current flow, measured in siemens (S).

front: What is the conductance of a 4 ohm part?
back: G = 1 / 4 = 0.25 siemens.

front: Convert 4.7 kilohms to ohms.
Convert 250 mA to amperes.
Convert 36 microamperes to amperes.
What do the prefixes mega, kilo, milli, and micro mean?
back: Mega is 1,000,000, kilo is 1,000, milli is 0.001, and micro is 0.000001.

front: Why estimate an answer before calculating?
back: A quick estimate catches decimal and power-of-ten mistakes. For example, 120 V across 12 ohms should be about 10 A.

front: What is the difference between DC and AC?
back: DC flows in one direction. AC reverses direction regularly, and in North America it completes 60 cycles per second.

front: How many times per second does 60 Hz AC change direction?
back: 120 times, since each cycle has two reversals.

front: Why do utilities use AC?
back: Transformers can easily raise and lower its voltage, so power can travel far at high voltage and be stepped down for use.

front: What does the 120 V rating of a receptacle mean for AC?
back: It is the RMS (effective) value, the DC voltage that gives the same heating effect. The AC peak is about 170 V.

front: What voltage appears across an open switch in a closed-loop 12 V circuit?
back: The full source voltage, 12 V, because the open contacts carry the whole supply.

front: State Ohm's law in its three forms.
back: I = V / R, V = I x R, and R = V / I.

front: What happens to current if voltage doubles and resistance is fixed?
back: Current doubles, since current is directly proportional to voltage.

front: What happens to current if resistance doubles and voltage is fixed?
back: Current is cut in half, since current is inversely proportional to resistance.

front: Find the current of a 24 V coil with 80 ohms of resistance.
Find the voltage across 9.6 ohms carrying 12.5 A.
Find the resistance of a 240 V element drawing 18.75 A.
What is a short circuit in terms of Ohm's law?
back: A path of very low resistance, so current rises toward the maximum the source can deliver unless protection opens it.

front: Why does a bulb often fail at switch-on?
back: A tungsten filament's cold resistance is about one tenth of its hot value, so the starting current surges.

front: What shortcut gives milliamperes from volts and kilohms?
back: Volts divided by kilohms gives milliamperes. For example, 12 V across 4 kilohms is 3 mA.

front: What is power and what is its unit?
back: The rate of doing work or using energy, measured in watts. One watt is one joule per second.

front: Write the basic electrical power formula.
back: P = V x I, power in watts equals volts times amperes.

front: Find the power of a 120 V heater drawing 12.5 A.
Give the three forms of the power equation.
back: P = V x I, P = I squared x R, and P = V squared / R.

front: Why does doubling the current quadruple the heat in a wire?
back: Power in a resistance is I squared times R, so doubling I multiplies it by four.

front: Find the heat in a 0.25 ohm connection carrying 16 A.
Find the resistance of a 4,000 W, 240 V element.
back: R = V squared / P = 57,600 / 4,000 = 14.4 ohms.

front: What power does a 240 V, 4,000 W element give on 208 V?
back: About 3,004 W, since power scales with the voltage ratio squared (0.867 squared is 0.751).

front: Find the current of a 4,000 W, 240 V element.
Why do resistors need a power rating at least double the calculated heat?
back: A margin prevents overheating and shortens failure risk, especially in hot enclosures.

front: What power does a 220 ohm resistor dissipate on 12 V?
back: P = 144 / 220 = 0.65 W, so choose a 1 W or preferably 2 W part.

front: What is a kilowatt-hour?
back: The energy used by a 1,000 W load running for one hour, equal to 3,600,000 joules.

front: Write the formula for energy in kilowatt-hours.
back: Energy (kWh) = power (kW) x time (hours).

front: How much energy does a 60 W lamp use in 50 hours?
back: 0.06 kW x 50 h = 3 kWh.

front: Find the cost of a 2.5 kW heater for 6 hours at $0.15 per kWh.
back: Energy is 15 kWh, so cost is 15 x 0.15 = $2.25.

front: What is the difference between a kilowatt and a kilowatt-hour?
back: A kilowatt is a rate of power. A kilowatt-hour is an amount of energy used over time.

front: How many watts are in one horsepower?
back: 746 watts.

front: What is the output of a 5 hp motor in watts?
Write the efficiency formula.
back: Efficiency = output power / input power x 100 percent. It is always below 100 percent.

front: Find the efficiency of a motor with 3,730 W output and 4,200 W input.
back: 3,730 / 4,200 x 100 = 88.8 percent, with 470 W lost as heat.

front: What counts as a continuous load, and how is it limited?
back: A load expected to run three hours or more. It should not exceed 80 percent of the breaker rating, so 12 A on 15 A and 16 A on 20 A.

front: Can a 1,500 W, 120 V heater run continuously on a 15 A circuit?
back: No. It draws 12.5 A, which exceeds the 12 A continuous limit.

front: What defines a series connection?
back: Parts are connected end to end so there is only one path for current. Cutting the path anywhere stops the current everywhere.

front: What is true of current in a series circuit?
back: It is the same through every part: I(total) = I1 = I2 = I3.

front: How do you find total resistance in series?
back: Add the resistances: R(total) = R1 + R2 + R3.

front: Find the total of 220, 330, and 470 ohms in series.
How does total series resistance compare with the largest single resistor?
back: It is always larger than the largest single resistor.

front: What is a voltage drop?
back: The voltage across a resistor as current passes through it, found from V = I x R.

front: State Kirchhoff's voltage law.
back: The voltage drops around a closed loop add up to the source voltage, or the sum of rises and drops around a loop is zero.

front: Find the current: 12 V across 100, 220, and 330 ohms in series.
back: Total R = 650 ohms, so I = 12 / 650 = 18.46 mA.

front: What are the three drops in that 12 V circuit?
back: 1.846 V, 4.062 V, and 6.092 V, which add up to 12.000 V.

front: Which resistor in a series circuit gets the largest voltage?
back: The largest resistance, since V = I x R with the same current.

front: State the voltage divider rule.
back: V(x) = V(source) x R(x) / R(total).

front: Find the voltage across 300 ohms in series with 100 ohms on 12 V.
back: 12 x 300 / 400 = 9 V, with 3 V across the 100 ohm resistor.

front: Why does a load change a voltage divider's output?
back: The load is in parallel with part of the divider, which lowers that part's resistance and the output voltage.

front: Which power formula is easiest in a series circuit and why?
back: P = I squared x R, because the current is common to all the resistors.

front: How does total power relate to part powers in series?
back: Total power equals the sum of the individual powers and also equals V(source) x I.

front: Find the power in 10 ohm and 30 ohm resistors in series on 40 V.
back: Current is 1 A. The 10 ohm part uses 10 W, the 30 ohm part uses 30 W, and the total is 40 W.

front: What mistake gives 53.3 W for the 30 ohm resistor?
back: Using the full 40 V in V squared / R. Only 30 V appears across that resistor.

front: How do voltages of cells in series combine?
back: They add when connected plus to minus. A cell reversed subtracts.

front: What do four 1.5 V cells in series give, and what if one is backward?
back: 6 V normally. With one backward the total is 1.5 + 1.5 + 1.5 - 1.5 = 3 V.

front: What is an open circuit in a series circuit?
back: A break in the path. Current falls to zero everywhere, and the open shows the full source voltage.

front: A voltmeter across a switch reads 24 V and across other parts reads 0. What is the fault?
back: The switch is open, because the full supply appears across the only open part.

front: What happens when one part of a series circuit shorts?
back: Its drop becomes zero, total resistance falls, current rises, and the other parts share the full supply.

front: Ten 12 V lamps in series on 120 V, one shorts. What voltage do the others get?
back: 120 / 9 = 13.3 V each, about 11 percent over their rating.

front: Why is wire resistance a series resistance?
back: The conductors are in the same single path as the load, so the load voltage is less than the supply.

front: Find the load voltage: 240 V, 20 ohm load, 0.4 ohm of wire.
back: Total 20.4 ohms, I = 11.76 A, load voltage = 11.76 x 20 = 235.3 V.

front: How much power does that wire waste?
back: I squared x R = 11.76 squared x 0.4 = 55.3 W.

front: What voltage drop does the NEC informational note recommend as a maximum?
back: 5 percent total for a feeder plus branch circuit, with no more than 3 percent in either. These are recommendations, not general requirements.

front: Why are safety interlocks wired in series?
back: Opening any one device drops out the relay coil and stops the machine, a fail-safe behavior.

front: Why are building loads not wired in series?
back: One open would shut off everything and each load would get a different share of the voltage.

front: What is internal resistance of a source?
back: A small resistance inside a battery in series with the load. The terminal voltage falls as load current rises.

front: What reading helps find an intermittent series fault?
back: Measure voltage across each connection under load. A drop of more than a few tenths of a volt where none belongs marks the culprit.

front: What defines a parallel connection?
back: Each part has its own path between the same two points, so removing one leaves the others working.

front: What is the same across every parallel branch?
back: The voltage, which equals the source voltage.

front: How do you find each branch current in parallel?
back: Apply Ohm's law to each branch: I = V / R.

front: State Kirchhoff's current law.
back: The current flowing into a junction equals the current flowing out, so branch currents add to the total.

front: Find the branch currents of 24, 40, and 60 ohm heaters on 120 V.
back: 5 A, 3 A, and 2 A, giving a total of 10 A.

front: A feeder gives 12 A to three branches. Two carry 4.5 A and 3.5 A. What is the third?
Write the reciprocal formula for parallel resistance.
How does total parallel resistance compare with the smallest branch?
back: It is always less than the smallest branch.

front: Find the total resistance of 24, 40, and 60 ohms in parallel.
Write the product over sum rule and say when it applies.
back: R(total) = (R1 x R2) / (R1 + R2). It works for two resistors at a time.

front: Find 30 ohms in parallel with 20 ohms.
What is the total resistance of N equal resistors in parallel?
back: R(total) = R / N.

front: Four 48 ohm sections in parallel on 240 V. Find total resistance and current.
back: R(total) = 12 ohms and I = 240 / 12 = 20 A.

front: What is 10 ohms in parallel with 10,000 ohms?
back: About 9.99 ohms. The large resistor changes almost nothing.

front: How do conductances combine in parallel?
back: They add directly: G(total) = G1 + G2 + G3.

front: State the current divider rule for two branches.
back: I1 = I(total) x R2 / (R1 + R2). The lower resistance carries the larger share.

front: 15 A splits between 10 and 20 ohm branches. What is each current?
back: 10 A in the 10 ohm branch and 5 A in the 20 ohm branch.

front: What is a meter shunt?
back: A very low resistance in parallel with a meter movement so only a small known fraction of a large current passes through it.

front: Find the shunt for a 1 mA, 50 ohm movement to read 10 A full scale.
back: Shunt carries 9.999 A at 0.05 V, so R = 0.05 / 9.999, about 0.005 ohm.

front: Which power formula is convenient in parallel and why?
back: P = V squared / R, because every branch has the same voltage.

front: Find the power in 24, 40, and 60 ohm branches on 120 V.
back: 600 W, 360 W, and 240 W, totaling 1,200 W.

front: What happens when one parallel branch opens?
back: Only that branch stops. The others keep full voltage and current, and total current falls.

front: What happens if the common conductor ahead of the junction opens?
back: Every branch loses power at once, so troubleshooting looks back toward the source.

front: Why is a short across one branch dangerous?
back: Total resistance falls toward zero and current rises toward the source limit, so the breaker must open quickly.

front: A 12 ohm load has a 0.5 ohm fault across it. What is the combined resistance?
back: 12 x 0.5 / 12.5 = 0.48 ohm, so current tries to reach 250 A on 120 V.

front: What happens to total current as loads are added to a branch circuit?
back: Total resistance falls and total current rises until the breaker may trip.

front: Find total current: 1,500 W, 1,100 W, and 600 W loads on 120 V.
How is a voltmeter connected, and why is its resistance high?
back: In parallel across the part. High internal resistance keeps it from drawing current and disturbing the circuit.

front: Why do lights dim when a big motor starts?
back: Starting current flows through wire resistance in series with the parallel loads, and the larger voltage drop reduces voltage at the lights.

front: What happens when two 12 V batteries are connected in parallel?
back: Voltage stays 12 V but capacity in ampere-hours doubles. The cells should match in voltage and charge.

front: Compare series and parallel for current and voltage.
back: In series, current is the same and voltage divides. In parallel, voltage is the same and current divides.

front: What is a combination circuit?
back: A circuit that contains both series and parallel connections. It is solved by reducing groups to equivalent resistors.

front: Which other name is used for a combination circuit?
back: A series-parallel circuit.

front: What is a node?
back: A point where two or more components connect. Labeling nodes with letters helps you spot series and parallel groups.

front: How do you test whether two resistors are in parallel?
back: Check that both ends of one connect to the same two nodes as the ends of the other. If so, they share the same voltage.

front: How do you test whether two resistors are in series?
back: They connect at a point where nothing else attaches, so the same current must pass through both.

front: Which formula gives two resistors in parallel?
back: R equivalent = (R1 x R2) / (R1 + R2), the product over the sum.

front: What is the reciprocal method for parallel resistors?
back: 1/R equivalent = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 and so on. Invert the total to get R equivalent.

front: Calculate 30 ohms in parallel with 60 ohms.
Why is a parallel equivalent always smaller than the smallest branch?
back: Each added path gives current another route, so total opposition falls below that of any single path.

front: In what order do you reduce a combination circuit?
back: Work from the innermost series or parallel group outward, replacing each with one equivalent resistor until a single resistor remains.

front: After reducing to one resistor, what is the next step?
back: Find total current with I = V / R, then expand the circuit back out to find each voltage and current.

front: A 10 ohm resistor is in series with 30 and 60 ohm resistors in parallel on 120 V. What is the total current?
back: Parallel pair = 20 ohms, total = 30 ohms, so I = 120 / 30 = 4 A.

front: In that circuit, what is the voltage across the 10 ohm resistor?
back: V = I x R = 4 A x 10 ohms = 40 V.

front: In that circuit, what voltage is across each parallel resistor?
back: 120 V - 40 V = 80 V, the same across both branches.

front: In that circuit, what are the branch currents?
back: 80 / 30 = 2.67 A and 80 / 60 = 1.33 A, which add to the 4 A total.

front: What does Kirchhoff's voltage law say?
back: The voltage drops around any closed loop add up to the source voltage.

front: What does Kirchhoff's current law say?
back: The current entering a junction equals the current leaving it.

front: Which resistor in a parallel group dissipates the most power?
back: The lowest-resistance one, because it carries the most current at the same voltage.

front: Name three formulas for resistor power.
back: P = V x I, P = I squared x R, and P = V squared / R.

front: What happens to total current if one parallel branch opens?
back: Total resistance rises, so total current falls.

front: What happens to the voltage on the surviving branch when a parallel branch opens?
back: It rises, because the series resistor now drops less voltage.

front: What happens to current when a parallel resistor shorts?
back: The short bypasses the other branches, resistance collapses, and current rises sharply, possibly opening a fuse.

front: A 4 ohm resistor is in series with 20 ohm and 30 ohm branches in parallel on 24 V. What is the total resistance?
back: 20 x 30 / 50 = 12 ohms, plus 4 ohms = 16 ohms.

front: What is the total power if a source delivers 4 A at 120 V to a combination circuit?
back: P = 120 x 4 = 480 W, equal to the sum of all resistor powers.

front: What is a voltage divider?
back: Two resistors in series used to produce a lower output voltage taken across one of them.

front: What is the divider output formula?
back: V out = V source x R bottom / (R top + R bottom).

front: A 12 V divider has two 1 kilohm resistors. What is the unloaded output?
What happens when a 1 kilohm load is attached across the lower resistor of that divider?
back: The lower leg becomes 500 ohms, so V out = 12 x 500 / 1,500 = 4 V.

front: How large should a divider load be to keep the output near its unloaded value?
back: At least about ten times the lower divider resistor.

front: Why do voltmeters have very high internal resistance?
back: So they act as a large load in parallel and barely disturb the circuit being measured.

front: What three checks confirm a combination circuit solution?
back: Loop voltages add to the source, branch currents add to the total, and resistor powers add to the source power.

front: What is a conductor?
back: A material that passes current easily because it has many loosely held outer electrons, such as copper or aluminum.

front: What is an insulator?
back: A material that holds its electrons tightly and resists current, such as rubber, plastic, glass or porcelain.

front: Why does a conductor's resistance matter in practice?
back: It causes voltage drop and heat, since P = I squared x R.

front: What does one circular mil measure?
back: The area of a circle 1 mil (0.001 inch) in diameter.

front: How do you find the area of a round wire in circular mils?
back: Square its diameter in mils: CM = d squared. No factor of pi is needed.

front: A wire is 0.080 inch across. What is its area in circular mils?
back: 80 mils squared = 6,400 circular mils.

front: How do you convert square mils to circular mils?
back: Divide by 0.7854 (multiply by 1.273).

front: In AWG, does a smaller number mean a thicker or thinner wire?
back: Thicker. 8 AWG is larger than 12 AWG, which is larger than 14 AWG.

front: How does area change for every three AWG numbers?
back: It roughly doubles going down in number (halves going up), and resistance changes inversely.

front: How does diameter change for every six AWG numbers?
back: It roughly doubles going down in number.

front: What is the area of 12 AWG in circular mils?
back: About 6,530 circular mils.

front: What is the area of 10 AWG in circular mils?
back: About 10,380 circular mils.

front: What is the area of 14 AWG in circular mils?
back: About 4,110 circular mils.

front: What does kcmil mean?
back: Thousands of circular mils, the unit used for conductors larger than 4/0, such as 250 kcmil.

front: Write the formula for conductor resistance.
back: R = K x L / CM, with L in feet and CM in circular mils.

front: What working K values are used for copper and aluminum at 75 degrees C?
back: About 12.9 for copper and 21.2 for aluminum.

front: Calculate the resistance of 250 ft of 14 AWG copper.
About how much more area does aluminum need than copper for equal resistance?
back: About 1.64 times, from 21.2 / 12.9.

front: Why must voltage drop calculations include the return conductor?
back: Current travels out and back, so the loop length is twice the one-way distance.

front: What is the single-phase voltage drop formula?
back: VD = 2 x K x I x L / CM, with L the one-way length in feet.

front: Find the drop for 16 A over 100 ft of 12 AWG copper at K = 12.9.
back: 2 x 12.9 x 16 x 100 / 6,530 = 6.32 V, which is 5.3 percent of 120 V.

front: What voltage drop target is commonly suggested for branch circuits?
back: About 3 percent, from an informational note in the NEC rather than a requirement.

front: What happens to copper resistance as it heats?
back: It rises, by about 0.393 percent per degree C near 20 degrees C.

front: Give the temperature and resistance formula.
back: R2 = R1 x [1 + alpha x (T2 - T1)], with alpha about 0.00393 per degree C for copper.

front: A 5.00 ohm copper coil is heated from 20 to 70 degrees C. What is its new resistance?
What is ampacity?
back: The maximum current a conductor can carry continuously without exceeding its temperature rating.

front: Which NEC table lists general conductor ampacities?
back: Table 310.16, with columns for 60, 75 and 90 degree C insulation.

front: What does Section 240.4(D) limit for small copper conductors?
back: Overcurrent protection: 15 A for 14 AWG, 20 A for 12 AWG, and 30 A for 10 AWG.

front: Six current-carrying 12 AWG THHN conductors share a conduit. What is the adjusted ampacity?
What do the letters T, H, W and N mean in THWN?
back: Thermoplastic, heat resistant, wet rated, and nylon jacketed.

front: Which insulation colors mark the grounded and the equipment grounding conductors?
back: White or gray for the grounded conductor, green, green with a yellow stripe or bare for the equipment ground.

front: What is a resistor?
back: A component made to have a specific resistance, used to limit current, divide voltage or produce heat.

front: What is a wirewound resistor best suited for?
back: High power jobs such as dropping resistors, braking and load banks, because the coil handles many watts.

front: What does resistor tolerance tell you?
back: How far the true value may stray from the marked value, as a percentage.

front: What is the acceptable range for a 4,700 ohm resistor with 5 percent tolerance?
Give the three power formulas for a resistor.
back: P = V x I, P = I squared x R, and P = V squared / R.

front: A 330 ohm resistor is rated 1/4 W and sits across 12 V. Is it safe?
back: P = 144 / 330 = 0.44 W, which exceeds 0.25 W, so it will overheat.

front: What margin is a good habit when picking a resistor power rating?
back: Choose at least double the calculated dissipation.

front: What are the digits of the resistor color code from 0 to 9?
back: Black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, gray 8, white 9.

front: In a four-band resistor, what do the bands mean?
back: Two digits, then a multiplier, then tolerance.

front: What tolerance do gold and silver bands mean?
back: Gold is plus or minus 5 percent and silver is plus or minus 10 percent.

front: Read yellow, violet, red, gold.
back: 47 x 100 = 4,700 ohms (4.7 kilohms) plus or minus 5 percent.

front: Read brown, black, orange, silver.
back: 10 x 1,000 = 10 kilohms plus or minus 10 percent, so 9,000 to 11,000 ohms.

front: Read the five-band resistor brown, green, black, red, brown.
back: 150 x 100 = 15 kilohms plus or minus 1 percent.

front: Why measure a resistor out of circuit?
back: Other parts in parallel would give a lower reading than the resistor's true value.

front: What is a potentiometer?
back: A three-terminal variable resistor with a sliding wiper, used as an adjustable voltage divider.

front: A linear potentiometer across 12 V has its wiper one quarter up from ground. What is the output?
back: 12 x 0.25 = 3 V, unloaded.

front: What is a rheostat?
back: A variable resistor wired with two terminals to control current.

front: What does a negative temperature coefficient thermistor do?
back: Its resistance falls as temperature rises.

front: What do poles and throws mean in a switch?
back: A pole is a separate circuit path, and a throw is a position the pole can connect to.

front: What is an SPDT switch used for?
back: One common terminal connects to either of two others, as in a three-way switch.

front: What is the difference between normally open and normally closed contacts?
back: Normally open contacts are apart at rest, and normally closed contacts touch at rest.

front: Why are DC switch ratings lower than AC ratings?
back: DC has no zero crossing, so the opening arc is harder to extinguish.

front: Which conductor should an ordinary switch open?
back: The ungrounded (hot) conductor.

front: What does a voltmeter read across a closed switch?
back: Nearly 0 V, because closed contacts have almost no resistance.

front: A lamp is dark, the switch is ON, and 120 V reads across the switch. What is wrong?
back: The contacts are not closing, so the switch is bad.

front: What is the difference between an overload and a short circuit?
back: An overload is a moderate excess current lasting some time, while a short circuit is a very large fault current.

front: Why should you never replace a fuse with a larger one?
back: The fuse is sized to protect the wire, and a larger one lets the wire overheat before opening.

front: What does a thermal-magnetic breaker contain?
back: A bimetal strip for slow overloads and an electromagnet for instant short-circuit tripping.

front: What does a GFCI sense and at what level does it trip?
back: A difference between hot and neutral current of about 4 to 6 milliamperes.

front: Size a breaker for a 4,500 W, 240 V water heater.
back: I = 18.75 A, x 1.25 = 23.4 A, so use a 25 A breaker with 10 AWG copper.

front: What does the interrupting rating of a breaker mean?
back: The largest fault current a device can safely open without being destroyed.

front: What is the difference between a cell and a battery?
back: A cell is a single unit converting chemical energy to electrical energy. A battery is a group of cells connected together.

front: What three parts make up every cell?
back: Two electrodes (positive and negative) and an electrolyte between them.

front: What determines a cell's voltage?
back: Its chemistry, not its size. AAA and D alkaline cells are both about 1.5 V.

front: What is a primary cell?
back: A single-use cell whose reaction cannot be practically reversed, such as an alkaline cell.

front: What is a secondary cell?
back: A rechargeable cell restored by pushing current backward through it.

front: Give nominal voltages for alkaline, lead-acid, NiMH and lithium-ion cells.
back: 1.5 V, 2.0 V, 1.2 V, and 3.6 to 3.7 V per cell.

front: What is the nominal voltage of one LiFePO4 cell?
back: About 3.2 V.

front: How many cells are in a 12 V lead-acid battery?
back: Six cells in series, about 2.1 V each when full, giving about 12.6 V.

front: What are the plates and electrolyte in a lead-acid cell?
back: Lead dioxide positive plate, sponge lead negative plate, in dilute sulfuric acid.

front: What happens to the acid as a lead-acid cell discharges?
back: It weakens, since both plates turn to lead sulfate and the electrolyte becomes more like water.

front: What does VRLA stand for and which types does it include?
back: Valve-regulated lead-acid, covering AGM and gel batteries.

front: What specific gravity does a fully charged lead-acid cell read?
back: About 1.265.

front: What tool measures specific gravity?
back: A hydrometer, usable only on flooded batteries with removable caps.

front: Give rested open-circuit voltages for a 12 V flooded battery at 100, 75, 50 and 25 percent charge.
What is sulfation?
back: Hardening of lead sulfate crystals on plates of a battery left discharged, permanently cutting capacity.

front: What does ampere-hour measure?
back: Charge capacity: one ampere flowing for one hour.

front: How do you find stored energy in watt-hours?
back: Volts x ampere-hours.

front: How much energy is in a 12 V, 100 Ah battery?
Why does a larger current drain give less total capacity?
back: Internal losses and chemistry limits rise with current, the Peukert effect.

front: What depth of discharge is a common routine limit for lead-acid?
back: About 50 percent of rated capacity.

front: A 12 V, 100 Ah battery with 50 percent usable runs a 240 W load with no losses. How long?
back: I = 20 A, usable 50 Ah, so 50 / 20 = 2.5 hours.

front: Why include inverter efficiency in a runtime estimate?
back: The inverter draws more DC power than it delivers, so omitting a 90 percent efficiency overstates runtime by about 10 percent.

front: State the terminal voltage formula under load.
back: V terminal = EMF - I x r, where r is internal resistance.

front: A 12.6 V battery has r = 0.025 ohm and supplies 120 A. What is the terminal voltage?
Why does a weak battery light the lamps but fail to start an engine?
back: Its internal resistance is high, so heavy starter current drops the terminal voltage too low.

front: What happens to voltage and capacity when batteries are connected in series?
back: Voltages add and ampere-hours stay the same.

front: What happens to voltage and capacity when batteries are connected in parallel?
back: Voltage stays the same and ampere-hours add.

front: Four 12 V, 100 Ah batteries are wired as two series strings in parallel. What are the bank's voltage and energy?
What are the typical float voltages for a 12 V lead-acid battery?
back: About 13.5 to 13.8 V, with 14.4 to 14.8 V in bulk and absorption stages.

front: Which order should you use to disconnect a vehicle battery?
back: Negative terminal first, and reconnect it last, to avoid a wrench short through the body.

front: Why is charging a flooded battery a fire and explosion hazard?
back: It releases hydrogen, which is explosive in air above about 4 percent.

front: State the first law of magnetism.
back: Unlike poles attract and like poles repel.

front: Which way do magnetic field lines run outside a magnet?
back: From the north pole to the south pole, forming closed loops that never cross.

front: What happens if you cut a bar magnet in half?
back: You get two smaller magnets, each with its own north and south pole.

front: Name the main ferromagnetic materials.
back: Iron, nickel and cobalt, plus some alloys.

front: What are magnetic domains?
back: Tiny regions where atomic magnets point the same way. Aligned domains make a magnet.

front: Why is soft iron used for relay and transformer cores?
back: It magnetizes easily and loses nearly all magnetism when the field is removed.

front: What is the Curie temperature?
back: The temperature above which a material loses its magnetism. It is about 770 degrees C for iron.

front: Define magnetic flux and give its unit.
back: The total number of field lines through an area, measured in webers (Wb).

front: Define flux density and give its unit and formula.
back: Flux per unit area, B = flux / A, in tesla (T) where 1 T = 1 Wb per square meter.

front: How many gauss equal one tesla?
back: 10,000 gauss.

front: Find the flux density for 0.0016 Wb through 0.002 square meters.
Who showed in 1820 that current produces a magnetic field?
back: Hans Christian Oersted, when a compass needle moved near a wire carrying current.

front: State the right-hand rule for a straight conductor.
back: Thumb along conventional current, curled fingers show the direction of the field circles.

front: State the right-hand rule for a coil.
back: Curl fingers in the direction of conventional current and the thumb points to the north pole.

front: What is magnetomotive force and its unit?
back: mmf = N x I, the cause of flux in a magnetic circuit, in ampere-turns.

front: Find the mmf of 800 turns carrying 1.5 A.
back: 800 x 1.5 = 1,200 ampere-turns.

front: What is field intensity H?
back: H = N x I / path length, in ampere-turns per meter.

front: Find H for 1,200 ampere-turns over 0.25 m.
back: 1,200 / 0.25 = 4,800 ampere-turns per meter.

front: What is permeability?
back: A measure of how easily a material supports magnetic flux. B = permeability x H.

front: Why does an air gap weaken an electromagnet?
back: Air has very high reluctance, so the same mmf drives much less flux.

front: What is magnetic saturation?
back: The point where nearly all domains are aligned and more mmf adds little flux.

front: What is hysteresis?
back: The lag of flux density behind the applied magnetizing force, which wastes energy as heat each cycle.

front: What is residual magnetism?
back: Magnetism a core keeps after the current is turned off.

front: Why are transformer cores laminated?
back: Thin insulated sheets break the paths of eddy currents, which cut heat loss.

front: Give the formula for force on a conductor in a field.
back: F = B x I x l, with the conductor at right angles to the field.

front: Find the force on 0.20 m of conductor carrying 25 A in a 0.8 T field.
Do parallel conductors with opposite currents attract or repel?
back: They repel. Same-direction currents attract.

front: Give the induced voltage in a moving conductor.
back: e = B x l x v, with the conductor moving at right angles to the field.

front: A 0.40 m conductor moves at 5 m/s across a 0.6 T field. What voltage is induced?
State Faraday's law for a coil, and find the voltage for 150 turns with a 0.006 Wb change in 0.03 s.
back: e = N x change in flux / change in time = 150 x 0.2 = 30 V.

front: State Lenz's law.
back: An induced current flows in a direction that opposes the change that produced it.

front: How is a voltmeter connected?
back: In parallel, with one lead on each side of the part being measured.

front: How is an ammeter connected?
back: In series, so the circuit current flows through the meter.

front: What happens if an ammeter is connected across a voltage source?
back: It acts as a near short circuit, which blows the meter fuse or causes an arc flash.

front: Why is an ohmmeter used only on a de-energized circuit?
back: It supplies its own test voltage, and outside voltage gives false readings or damages the meter.

front: What do CAT II, CAT III and CAT IV cover?
back: CAT II is outlets and plug-in loads, CAT III is panels, feeders and branch circuits, and CAT IV is the service entrance.

front: Why choose a meter with a CAT rating at or above the circuit?
back: It has been tested to survive the transient surges of sources with more available energy.

front: How does a d'Arsonval movement work?
back: A pivoted coil in a permanent magnet field twists in proportion to the current through it.

front: What is a typical digital voltmeter input resistance?
back: About 10 megohms.

front: What does accuracy of plus or minus (0.5 percent + 2 digits) mean?
back: Error equals 0.5 percent of the reading plus two steps of the last digit.

front: What is the error band on a 120.0 V reading at 0.5 percent + 2 digits (0.1 V per digit)?
Is resolution the same as accuracy?
back: No. A display can show 0.1 V steps and still be wrong by a volt.

front: A 10 V source feeds two 1 megohm resistors. What does a 10 megohm meter read across the lower one?
What reading would a 1 megohm meter give in that divider?
back: The lower leg becomes 0.5 megohm, so 10 x 0.5 / 1.5 = 3.33 V.

front: What does RMS mean?
back: The AC value that heats a resistor as much as the same amount of DC.

front: What is the peak of a 120 V RMS sine wave?
How is RMS found from a sine-wave peak?
back: RMS = peak x 0.707.

front: When do you need a true RMS meter?
back: On distorted waveforms from drives, LED drivers and computers, where average-responding meters read low.

front: What voltages are expected on a 120/240 V single-phase service?
back: About 120 V hot to neutral and about 240 V between the two hots.

front: What does 120 V hot to ground but 0 V hot to neutral suggest?
back: An open neutral.

front: How does an AC clamp meter sense current?
back: The split iron core acts as a transformer, with the conductor as a one-turn primary.

front: How does a DC clamp meter work?
back: It uses a Hall effect sensor to sense the steady magnetic field.

front: Why does a clamp around both hot and neutral read near zero?
back: The equal and opposite currents produce fields that cancel.

front: How can a clamp around all circuit conductors find a ground leak?
back: Any imbalance is current leaking to ground, so it reads the leakage current.

front: What resistance does a 1,000 W, 120 V element have when hot?
back: R = V squared / P = 14,400 / 1,000 = 14.4 ohms.

front: Why does a cold incandescent lamp measure far lower than its hot resistance?
back: Tungsten resistance rises with temperature. A 100 W lamp is about 144 ohms hot and only about 10 to 15 ohms cold.

front: Why can a resistor reading in circuit be lower than its true value?
back: Other components form parallel paths, so the reading is at most the true value.

front: Why can a continuity beep be misleading?
back: It shows a path exists, not that its resistance is low enough for the load.

front: Why can an ordinary ohmmeter not test insulation?
back: Its test voltage is too low. A megohmmeter applies 500 V or more.

front: What series multiplier makes a 1 mA, 50 ohm movement read 10 V full scale?
back: 10 / 0.001 = 10,000 ohms total, minus 50 gives 9,950 ohms.

front: How is a shunt chosen to extend an ammeter range?
back: The shunt carries the extra current at the same voltage as the movement. For 1 A from 1 mA and 50 ohms: 0.050 V / 0.999 A = about 0.05 ohm.

front: What is the live-dead-live method?
back: Test the meter on a known live source, test the circuit, then test the known source again.

front: What makes the voltage in a rotating loop of wire alternate?
back: Each side of the loop cuts the magnetic field in the opposite sense every half turn, so the induced voltage reverses direction. The voltage is proportional to the sine of the loop angle.

front: What is one cycle of an alternating voltage?
back: One complete set of values: zero, positive peak, zero, negative peak, back to zero. It spans 360 electrical degrees.

front: Define frequency and give its unit.
back: Frequency is the number of cycles per second. Its unit is the hertz (Hz), where 1 Hz equals one cycle per second.

front: What is the relationship between frequency and period?
back: They are reciprocals: f = 1 / T and T = 1 / f. Higher frequency means a shorter period.

front: Find the period of a 60 Hz supply.
Find the period of a 400 Hz aircraft supply.
An unknown waveform takes 8 ms per cycle. What is its frequency?
Write the formula for the frequency of a synchronous alternator.
back: f = (P x N) / 120, with P the number of poles, N the speed in rpm, and f in hertz.

front: At what speed must a four-pole alternator turn to make 60 Hz?
What speed does a four-pole alternator need to make 50 Hz?
A portable generator reads 58.2 Hz on a four-pole engine. What is its shaft speed?
back: N = 120 x 58.2 / 4 = 1,746 rpm, about 54 rpm below the correct 1,800 rpm.

front: What is the peak-to-peak value of a sine wave in terms of its peak?
back: Vpp = 2 x Vp.

front: What does the rms value of an AC voltage represent?
back: It is the direct voltage that would deliver the same power to a resistor. It is the number on meters and nameplates.

front: Give the conversion factors between rms and peak for a sine wave.
back: Vrms = 0.707 x Vp, and Vp = 1.414 x Vrms.

front: What is the average value of a half cycle of a sine wave?
back: Vavg = 0.637 x Vp. The average over a full cycle is zero.

front: Find the peak voltage of a 120 V rms outlet.
back: Vp = 1.414 x 120 = 169.7 V. The peak-to-peak value is 339.4 V.

front: What peak voltage does a 240 V rms circuit reach?
Why does using peak voltage in a power formula give a wrong answer?
back: The power formula needs the rms value. Using the peak (1.414 times larger) doubles the result, since the voltage is squared.

front: A 15 ohm heater is on 120 V rms. Find current and power.
What does it mean when one wave lags another by 90 degrees?
back: It reaches each point in its cycle one quarter cycle later than the other wave, which is 4.17 ms at 60 Hz.

front: Convert a phase angle to a time shift.
back: time shift = (angle / 360) x T. At 60 Hz, 45 degrees is 2.083 ms.

front: What is the phase relationship of voltage and current in a resistive circuit?
back: They are in phase, with zero phase angle.

front: Write the formula for the instantaneous value of a sine wave.
back: v = Vp x sin(theta), where theta is the angle in degrees from the zero crossing.

front: A wave has a 170 V peak. What is its value at 30 degrees?
A wave has a 200 V peak. What is its value at 40 degrees?
What is the angular velocity omega at 60 Hz?
back: omega = 2 x pi x f = 377 radians per second.

front: Why are the stationary windings of a large alternator placed on the stator?
back: The heavy output current then leaves through fixed cables instead of brushes. Only the small field current goes through slip rings or a brushless exciter.

front: What controls an alternator's output voltage, and what controls its frequency?
back: Voltage is controlled by the rotor field current. Frequency is controlled by the speed of the engine or turbine.

front: How does a 120/240 V split-phase service produce 240 V?
back: The two hot conductors are the ends of a center-tapped winding, 180 degrees apart, so their 120 V values add to 240 V. Each hot to neutral is 120 V.

front: A 4,800 W water heater runs on 240 V or 120 V. Compare the currents.
back: At 240 V it draws 20 A. At 120 V it would draw 40 A, needing heavier wire.

front: A scope shows 6 divisions peak to peak at 50 V per division. What is the rms voltage?
What is self-induction?
back: A changing current in a coil induces a voltage in that same coil, because its own changing field cuts its own turns.

front: State Lenz's law.
back: An induced voltage always has a polarity that opposes the change that caused it. A coil resists any change in its current.

front: Define the henry.
back: One henry is the inductance of a coil in which a current changing at one ampere per second induces one volt.

front: Write the formula for induced voltage in an inductor.
back: v = L x (change in i / change in t).

front: A 4 H coil carries 2 A, and the current falls to zero in 0.05 s. What voltage is induced?
A 0.25 H relay coil carries 0.4 A, and the current drops to zero in 2 ms. What voltage appears?
back: v = 0.25 x 0.4 / 0.002 = 50 V, even if the supply is only 24 V.

front: Write the formula for energy stored in an inductor.
back: W = 0.5 x L x I squared, in joules.

front: How much energy does a 2 H choke carrying 3 A store?
back: W = 0.5 x 2 x 9 = 9 joules.

front: How does the number of turns affect a coil's inductance?
back: Inductance increases with the square of the turns. Doubling the turns quadruples the inductance.

front: List the four factors that set the inductance of a coil.
back: Number of turns (squared), cross-sectional area, length (inverse), and the core permeability.

front: Write the inductance formula for a solenoid.
back: L = (mu x N squared x A) / l.

front: Find the inductance of a 500-turn air-core coil, 2 cm squared area, 0.1 m long.
Why do power-frequency inductors use iron cores?
back: Iron has a permeability hundreds or thousands of times that of air, so a manageable coil gets a large inductance.

front: What happens to an iron-core inductor when the core saturates?
back: Its permeability and inductance drop sharply, and the current can jump to a high value.

front: Write the RL time constant formula.
back: tau = L / R, in seconds. The current reaches 63.2 percent of its final value in one tau.

front: A coil of 0.5 H and 100 ohms is on 50 V DC. Find the time constant and final current.
back: tau = 0.5 / 100 = 5 ms. Final current = 50 / 100 = 0.5 A, reached in about 25 ms.

front: Why does opening a switch on an inductive load cause an arc?
back: The collapsing field induces a large voltage that tries to keep the current flowing across the opening contacts.

front: What is a flyback diode used for?
back: A diode across a relay coil gives the collapsing-field current a safe path, protecting the transistor or contact that switches the coil.

front: How do inductors combine in series?
back: L total = L1 + L2 + L3 + ... when their fields do not link.

front: Find the total of 1.5 H, 2.5 H and 4 H in series.
Find the total of 6 H and 3 H in parallel.
Define inductive reactance and give the formula.
back: XL is the opposition of a coil to AC, measured in ohms: XL = 2 x pi x f x L, or 377 x L at 60 Hz.

front: Find XL of a 0.2 H coil at 60 Hz.
Find XL of a 25 mH choke at 60 Hz and at 120 Hz.
back: 9.425 ohms at 60 Hz and 18.85 ohms at 120 Hz.

front: How does inductive reactance change with frequency?
back: It rises in direct proportion to frequency, and is zero at DC.

front: A 0.5 H coil is on 120 V, 60 Hz. Find the current, ignoring resistance.
A coil on 240 V, 60 Hz draws 2.0 A with negligible resistance. Find L.
What is the phase relationship between voltage and current in a pure inductor?
back: The current lags the voltage by 90 degrees. The memory aid is ELI: E leads I in an inductor.

front: Does a pure inductor use real power?
back: No. It takes energy to build its field and returns it as the field collapses, so net power is zero. The back-and-forth power is reactive, in vars.

front: Why does an ohmmeter reading mislead you about a coil's AC current?
back: The ohmmeter sees only the wire resistance. On AC the reactance, often hundreds of ohms, sets most of the current.

front: Why does a stuck AC contactor coil burn out?
back: With the armature open, the air gap lowers the inductance and reactance, so the coil draws much more current than when closed.

front: What is a capacitor?
back: Two conductors separated by an insulating dielectric, storing energy in the electric field between them.

front: What does a charged capacitor do to direct current?
back: Once charged it blocks DC, since no current crosses the dielectric.

front: Define capacitance and write its formula.
back: Capacitance is the ability to store charge per volt: C = Q / V, in farads.

front: Define the farad.
back: One farad is the capacitance that stores one coulomb of charge at one volt.

front: Convert: microfarad, nanofarad, picofarad.
back: 1 uF = 10 to the minus 6 F, 1 nF = 10 to the minus 9 F, 1 pF = 10 to the minus 12 F.

front: A capacitor holds 3 mC at 12 V. What is its capacitance?
How much charge does a 220 uF capacitor hold at 50 V?
Write the energy stored in a capacitor.
back: W = 0.5 x C x V squared, in joules.

front: How much energy does a 220 uF capacitor store at 400 V?
What three features set the capacitance of a plate capacitor?
back: Plate area (more raises it), plate spacing (less raises it), and the dielectric permittivity.

front: Write the capacitance formula for parallel plates.
back: C = (epsilon0 x epsilon_r x A) / d, with epsilon0 = 8.854 x 10 to the minus 12 F/m.

front: Find the capacitance of two 0.01 m squared plates 1 mm apart in air.
What happens to capacitance if the plate spacing is halved?
back: It doubles.

front: Why must an AC capacitor's voltage rating exceed the rms voltage?
back: It must withstand the peak. A 240 V rms circuit peaks at 339 V, so a 250 V part is not adequate.

front: Write the RC time constant.
back: tau = R x C. The capacitor reaches 63.2 percent of the supply voltage in one tau and about 99 percent in five.

front: Find tau for 10 kilohms and 100 uF.
What is the voltage after one time constant in a 24 V RC charging circuit?
A 470 uF capacitor has a 100 kilohm bleeder. How long to discharge below 1 percent?
back: tau = 47 s, so five time constants is about 235 s.

front: How do capacitors combine in parallel?
back: C total = C1 + C2 + C3 + ...

front: Find the total of 10 uF, 22 uF and 47 uF in parallel.
back: 79 uF.

front: How do capacitors combine in series?
back: 1 / C total = 1 / C1 + 1 / C2 + ..., so the total is smaller than the smallest part.

front: Find 10 uF in series with 40 uF.
In a series capacitor string, which part takes the larger voltage?
back: The smaller capacitor, because the same charge flows and V = Q / C.

front: Define capacitive reactance and give its formula.
back: XC = 1 / (2 x pi x f x C), or 1 / (377 x C) at 60 Hz, in ohms.

front: Find XC of a 40 uF capacitor at 60 Hz.
Find XC of a 100 uF capacitor at 60 Hz and at 120 Hz.
back: 26.5 ohms at 60 Hz and 13.3 ohms at 120 Hz.

front: How does capacitive reactance change with frequency?
back: It falls as frequency rises, and is infinite at DC.

front: A 30 uF capacitor is on 240 V, 60 Hz. Find the current.
What is the phase relationship in a pure capacitor?
back: The current leads the voltage by 90 degrees. The memory aid is ICE: I leads E in a capacitor.

front: How should you discharge a large capacitor before servicing?
back: After lockout, connect an insulated, rated resistor across the terminals, then confirm near zero volts with a meter. Do not short it with a bare screwdriver.

front: Why is a start capacitor not a substitute for a run capacitor?
back: A start capacitor is rated for a few seconds of duty and overheats if left on, while a run capacitor is built for continuous duty.

front: Define impedance.
back: Impedance Z is the total opposition to AC from resistance and reactance, measured in ohms.

front: State Ohm's law for AC circuits.
back: I = V / Z, using rms values.

front: Why can't resistance and reactance be added directly?
back: They are 90 degrees apart in phase, so they combine like the legs of a right triangle.

front: Write the impedance formula from R and net reactance X.
back: Z = square root of (R squared + X squared).

front: How do you find the phase angle in an impedance triangle?
back: theta = arctan (X / R).

front: What are cos theta and sin theta in the impedance triangle?
back: cos theta = R / Z and sin theta = X / Z.

front: A series circuit has R = 30 and XL = 40. Find Z and the angle.
back: Z = 50 ohms and theta = 53.13 degrees, current lagging.

front: In a series RL circuit on 120 V with R = 30 and XL = 40, find the current and part voltages.
back: I = 2.4 A, VR = 72 V, VL = 96 V. They combine as the square root of (72 squared + 96 squared) = 120 V.

front: Why can the part voltages in a series reactive circuit exceed the supply?
back: They are out of phase and add as triangle sides, not arithmetically. Kirchhoff's law holds for phasors.

front: A coil of 8 ohms and 0.1 H is in series with a 22 ohm load on 120 V, 60 Hz. Find Z.
back: XL = 37.7 ohms, R total = 30 ohms, Z = 48.18 ohms.

front: What does a series RC circuit do to the phase relationship?
back: The current leads the supply voltage.

front: A 60 ohm resistor is in series with XC = 80 ohms on 240 V. Find Z and I.
back: Z = 100 ohms and I = 2.4 A.

front: Find the voltages in that RC circuit (60 ohm and XC = 80, I = 2.4 A).
back: VR = 144 V and VC = 192 V. The square root of the sum of squares is 240 V.

front: A 100 uF capacitor is in series with 15 ohms at 120 V, 60 Hz. Find Z.
back: XC = 26.5 ohms, Z = 30.45 ohms, I = 3.94 A.

front: How is net reactance found in a series RLC circuit?
back: X = XL minus XC. Positive means inductive, negative means capacitive.

front: Series RLC: R = 40, XL = 90, XC = 60. Find Z.
back: Net X = 30 ohms, Z = square root of (1,600 + 900) = 50 ohms.

front: For that circuit on 120 V, find the current and phase angle.
back: I = 2.4 A and theta = arctan (30 / 40) = 36.87 degrees, lagging.

front: In that circuit, what voltage is across the inductor?
back: VL = 2.4 x 90 = 216 V, almost twice the 120 V supply.

front: What is series resonance?
back: The condition in which XL equals XC, the net reactance is zero, and the impedance equals R.

front: Write the resonant frequency formula.
back: f0 = 1 / (2 x pi x square root of (L x C)).

front: Find f0 for 50 mH and 20 uF.
back: L x C = 10 to the minus 6, its square root is 0.001, so f0 = 159.2 Hz.

front: What happens to current at series resonance?
back: Impedance is a minimum (equal to R), so current is at its maximum, I = V / R.

front: What capacitance resonates a 1 H coil at 60 Hz?
back: C = 1 / (377 squared x 1) = 7.04 uF.

front: Why can resonance be a hazard in power systems?
back: A capacitor bank can resonate with system inductance near a harmonic, multiplying currents and voltages and blowing fuses.

front: In a parallel circuit, what is common and what differs?
back: Voltage is common to all branches and the branch currents differ.

front: Give the branch currents in a parallel RLC circuit.
back: IR = V / R, IL = V / XL, IC = V / XC.

front: Write the total current formula for a parallel RLC circuit.
back: IT = square root of (IR squared + (IL minus IC) squared).

front: Parallel RL on 120 V: R = 24, XL = 18. Find IT and Z.
Parallel RC on 120 V: R = 12, XC = 16. Find IT.
back: IR = 10 A, IC = 7.5 A, IT = 12.5 A, Z = 9.6 ohms, current leading.

front: Parallel RLC on 120 V: R = 60, XL = 40, XC = 120. Find IT.
back: IR = 2, IL = 3, IC = 1 A. Net reactive = 2 A, IT = 2.83 A, angle 45 degrees lagging.

front: How does parallel resonance differ from series resonance?
back: Impedance is a maximum and supply current a minimum when IL equals IC, the opposite of series resonance.

front: Name the three kinds of power in an AC circuit with units.
back: True power P in watts, reactive power Q in vars, apparent power S in volt-amperes.

front: What is true power?
back: The power actually converted to work or heat, in watts. It is what the utility meter bills.

front: What is reactive power?
back: Power that moves back and forth between the source and a coil's or capacitor's field. It does no net work and is measured in vars.

front: What is apparent power?
back: S = V x I in volt-amperes, with no regard for phase. Equipment must be sized to carry it.

front: Why are transformers and generators rated in kVA?
back: They must carry the full current, whatever part of it does useful work.

front: State the power triangle relationships.
back: S squared = P squared + Q squared, with P = V x I x cos theta and Q = V x I x sin theta.

front: Define power factor.
back: pf = P / S = cos theta, a number from 0 to 1.

front: When is power factor lagging, and when leading?
back: Lagging for an inductive load, where current lags voltage. Leading for a capacitive load.

front: A motor draws 20 A at 240 V with pf 0.8. Find S, P and Q.
Series R = 30 and X = 40 on 120 V draws 2.4 A. Find P, Q and S.
A load uses 6,000 W and 8,000 vars. Find the apparent power.
What is the power factor of a resistive load?
back: 1.0, since voltage and current are in phase and all power is true power.

front: What is the true power of a pure inductor or capacitor?
back: Zero. All of its power is reactive.

front: Why does a lightly loaded motor have a poor power factor?
back: Its magnetizing current is mostly reactive, so with little real work the power factor may be 0.2 to 0.3.

front: A 120 V motor draws 6 A and a wattmeter reads 480 W. Find the power factor.
Compute the current for 5 kW at 240 V at pf 1.0, 0.7 and 0.5.
Why does a low power factor cost money?
back: The same true power needs more current, which heats conductors with the square of the current, loads transformers and may bring utility penalties.

front: Which instrument measures true power?
back: A wattmeter or power meter. A voltmeter and an ammeter give only volt-amperes.

front: A compressor reads 238 V, 18.0 A and 3,450 W. Find the power factor.
What is the reactive power for that compressor?
back: Q = square root of (4,284 squared minus 3,450 squared) = about 2,540 vars.

front: How does a parallel capacitor correct power factor?
back: Its leading current cancels part of the motor's lagging reactive current, so the supply carries less current. The motor's real power is unchanged.

front: Write the capacitor size formula for power factor correction.
back: Qc = P x (tan theta1 minus tan theta2).

front: Correct 10 kW from pf 0.70 to 0.95. Find the capacitor kvar.
back: Q1 = 10.2 kvar, Q2 = 3.29 kvar, Qc = 6.9 kvar.

front: What current reduction does that correction bring at 240 V?
back: From 59.5 A to 43.9 A, about 26 percent less.

front: Convert kvar to microfarads for a single-phase load.
back: XC = V squared / Qc, then C = 1 / (2 x pi x f x XC). For 6.91 kvar at 240 V, C is about 318 uF.

front: Why should you avoid oversizing a power factor capacitor?
back: It can make the circuit leading, raise voltage, or self-excite a motor that is switched off while spinning.

front: Define efficiency of a motor.
back: Efficiency = output power / input power x 100 percent. 1 hp = 746 W.

front: A 5 hp motor draws 4,300 W. Find the efficiency.
back: Output = 3,730 W, so efficiency = 3,730 / 4,300 = 86.7 percent.

front: How is energy cost computed?
back: kWh = kW x hours, multiplied by the price. 3 kW for 4 h is 12 kWh, or $1.68 at 14 cents.

front: Does power factor correction reduce kWh used by a motor?
back: No. It reduces current and the losses and loading it causes, not the true energy used.

front: A 100 kW generator is rated at 0.8 pf. What is its kVA rating?
What is three-phase power?
back: Three equal voltages of the same frequency, spaced 120 electrical degrees apart, carried on three line conductors.

front: Give three advantages of three-phase power.
back: Constant total power, smaller conductors for the same power, and self-starting induction motors.

front: How much current does each three-phase conductor carry compared with single phase for equal power and line voltage?
back: About 58 percent, or 1 divided by 1.732.

front: How far apart in time are phases A and B at 60 Hz?
back: 120 degrees is 5.56 ms, and phase C follows at 11.11 ms.

front: What is phase sequence?
back: The order in which the phase voltages reach their peaks, such as ABC (positive sequence) or ACB.

front: How do you reverse a three-phase motor?
back: Interchange any two of the three line conductors at the motor.

front: Why use a phase sequence meter?
back: To check the rotation before connecting equipment, such as a scroll compressor, that can be destroyed by running backward.

front: Define phase voltage and line voltage.
back: Phase voltage is across one winding or load element. Line voltage is between two line conductors.

front: Give the wye connection relationships.
back: VL = 1.732 x Vph and IL = Iph.

front: Give the delta connection relationships.
back: VL = Vph and IL = 1.732 x Iph.

front: Find the line voltage when the phase voltage is 120 V in a wye.
Find the line voltage when the phase voltage is 277 V in a wye.
What does 208Y/120 mean?
back: A wye system with 208 V line to line and 120 V line to neutral.

front: What are 480Y/277 volt systems used for?
back: 277 V line to neutral for lighting, and 480 V three-phase for motors and large equipment.

front: Three 12 ohm resistors are wye-connected on 208 V. Find phase voltage, current and total power.
back: Vph = 120 V, I = 10 A, total power = 3 x 1,200 = 3,600 W.

front: Three 20 ohm resistors are delta-connected on 240 V. Find the line current and power.
How does delta power compare with wye power for the same resistors and line voltage?
back: Delta gives three times the power, since each element gets full line voltage instead of 58 percent.

front: What is a high-leg delta?
back: A 240 V delta with one winding center-tapped as neutral. The two lines on that winding are 120 V to neutral, and the high leg is 208 V to neutral.

front: How must the high-leg conductor be marked?
back: Orange or another effective means (NEC 110.15), usually in the B position.

front: Write the three-phase true power formula.
back: P = 1.732 x VL x IL x cos theta.

front: Write the three-phase apparent and reactive power formulas.
back: S = 1.732 x VL x IL and Q = 1.732 x VL x IL x sin theta.

front: A 208 V three-phase motor draws 25 A at pf 0.9. Find S and P.
Find the line current for a 15 kW resistive three-phase load at 480 V.
A 480 V motor draws 30 A at pf 0.85 and is 92 percent efficient. Find shaft horsepower.
back: P = 21,201 W input, 19,505 W output, about 26.1 hp.

front: What is the neutral current of a balanced three-phase wye load?
back: Zero, since the three equal currents 120 degrees apart sum to zero.

front: Find the neutral current for line currents of 40, 35 and 30 A.
back: IN = square root of (3,725 minus 3,650) = square root of 75 = 8.66 A.

front: Why is voltage unbalance harmful to a three-phase motor?
back: A small voltage unbalance causes a much larger current unbalance and overheats the rotor and windings.

front: Line voltages are 462, 471 and 477 V. Find the percent unbalance.
back: Average 470 V, maximum deviation 8 V, so 8 / 470 = 1.7 percent.

front: What is single phasing?
back: Loss of one supply phase while a motor runs. The motor draws high current in the other lines and can burn out within minutes.

front: A delta heater shows line currents of 14.4, 14.4 and 25.0 A. What is the fault?
back: One element is open, since two lines carry the phase current and one carries 1.732 times it.

front: What is the expected line current of a 9 kW, 208 V three-phase heater?
What two windings does a basic transformer have?
back: The primary winding receives energy from the source, and the secondary winding delivers energy to the load. They share a magnetic core but no electrical connection.

front: What principle lets a transformer work?
back: Mutual induction. A changing magnetic field made by the primary current induces a voltage in the secondary winding.

front: Why will a transformer not work on steady DC?
back: A steady current makes a steady field, and a field that does not change induces no secondary voltage. The primary can also overheat.

front: Why is a transformer core made of laminations?
back: Thin, insulated steel sheets confine eddy currents to small paths, which cuts heating and energy loss.

front: What are eddy currents?
back: Circulating currents induced in the core by the changing magnetic field. They produce heat and waste energy.

front: State the voltage and turns relationship.
back: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns. Voltage is in the same proportion as the number of turns.

front: A transformer has 600 primary turns and 150 secondary turns on 240 V. What is the secondary voltage?
back: Vs = 240 x 150 / 600 = 60 V. The 4 to 1 ratio divides the voltage by 4.

front: What is a step-down transformer?
back: One whose secondary has fewer turns than the primary, so the secondary voltage is lower than the primary voltage.

front: What is a step-up transformer?
back: One whose secondary has more turns than the primary, so the secondary voltage is higher than the primary voltage.

front: State the current relationship for an ideal transformer.
back: Ip / Is = Ns / Np. Current is inversely proportional to turns, and the low-voltage winding carries more current.

front: Which winding uses heavier wire, the high-voltage or the low-voltage side?
back: The low-voltage winding uses heavier wire because it carries more current. The high-voltage winding has more turns of finer wire.

front: Why are transformers rated in VA or kVA and not in watts?
back: Heating depends on winding current and voltage, not on the load's power factor, so the rating is in volt-amperes.

front: Find the full-load currents of a 5 kVA, 480 V to 120 V single-phase transformer.
What is core loss, and how does it vary with load?
back: Core loss, or iron loss, comes from eddy currents and magnetic reversal in the steel. It stays roughly constant from no load to full load.

front: What is copper loss, and how does it vary with load?
back: Copper loss is I squared R heating in the windings. It rises with the square of the load current.

front: If load current doubles, how does copper loss change?
back: It increases by a factor of four, because loss is proportional to current squared.

front: Write the efficiency formula.
back: Efficiency = (output power / input power) x 100, where input equals output plus losses.

front: A transformer outputs 4,800 W with 200 W of total loss. What is its efficiency?
back: Input = 5,000 W. Efficiency = 4,800 / 5,000 x 100 = 96 percent.

front: Define voltage regulation.
back: The percent change in secondary voltage from no load to full load, equal to (no-load minus full-load) / full-load x 100.

front: A secondary reads 245 V with no load and 240 V at full load. What is the regulation?
What is an autotransformer?
back: A transformer with a single winding tapped to give the secondary. Part of the winding is shared by input and output, and there is no isolation.

front: A 6 kVA autotransformer steps 480 V down to 240 V. What are the input and output currents?
back: Input: 6,000 / 480 = 12.5 A. Output: 6,000 / 240 = 25 A. The common winding carries 12.5 A.

front: What is a buck-boost transformer used for?
back: It adds to (boost) or subtracts from (buck) the supply voltage in series, to correct a slightly high or low voltage.

front: How are transformer terminals labeled?
back: H1 and H2 for the high-voltage side, and X1 and X2 for the low-voltage side.

front: How do you test additive or subtractive polarity?
back: Jumper H1 to X1, apply a safe voltage to the high winding, and measure H2 to X2. A reading higher than the applied voltage is additive, and lower is subtractive.

front: How does a dual-voltage 120/240 V secondary give both voltages?
back: Two equal windings in series give 240 V across the ends, and the center tie gives 120 V from either end to the neutral.

front: What is a tap on a transformer winding?
back: An extra connection point that changes the number of active turns, used to adjust the output voltage by a few percent.

front: What causes a large current surge when a transformer is first energized?
back: Inrush current, as the core is briefly driven into saturation. It can be many times the full-load current for a fraction of a second.

front: What does an ohmmeter reading of infinity across a winding indicate?
back: An open winding, which must be replaced or repaired. The winding is checked with the transformer de-energized and locked out.

front: What test finds weak insulation between a winding and the case?
back: An insulation resistance test with a megohmmeter. A low or falling reading indicates moisture or damaged insulation.

front: At what frequency does a transformer hum on a 60 Hz supply?
back: At 120 Hz, twice the supply frequency, because the magnetic force peaks twice per cycle.

front: In a wye connection, how are line voltage and phase voltage related?
back: Vline = 1.732 x Vphase. The line current equals the phase current.

front: In a delta connection, how are line current and phase current related?
back: Iline = 1.732 x Iphase. The line voltage equals the phase voltage.

front: What is the value of the square root of 3 used in three-phase work?
back: About 1.732.

front: What two choices exist for transforming three-phase power?
back: Three single-phase transformers wired as a bank, or one three-phase transformer with all windings on a single core.
